title: [B2 • Band 6.0] Bài 312: The Singing Hominin: Roots of Melody
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 312 (LEVEL B2 • BAND 6.0)

The Singing Hominin: The Evolutionary Roots of Melody

Paragraph 1. For centuries, Western thinkers viewed music as a pleasant cultural ornament invented long after spoken language. In The Descent of Man (1871), Charles Darwin challenged this view, proposing that musical vocalising came before speech as a courtship display similar to birdsong. Throughout most of the twentieth century, however, scientists rejected Darwin's hypothesis and treated music as a secondary accident. Cognitive scientist Steven Pinker famously labelled music 'auditory cheesecake'—a delightful indulgence that stimulates pleasure centres while offering zero biological survival value.

Paragraph 2. In The Singing Neanderthal, archaeologist Dr. Steven Mithen dismantles this dismissive consensus. Treating music as an evolutionary triviality ignores its universal presence across all human societies and its deep wiring in our brains. Infants respond to musical pitch and cadence months before understanding spoken grammar, and maternal 'motherese' relies on musical contours everywhere to soothe distress. Furthermore, neuroimaging confirms that listening to music activates archaic subcortical brain networks tied directly to emotion and social bonding.

Paragraph 3. Mithen proposes that language and music evolved from one shared ancestral system called Hmmmmm—standing for Holistic, multi-modal, manipulative, musical, and mimetic. Before abstract grammar existed, extinct hominins such as Homo heidelbergensis and Neanderthals communicated using expressive melodic calls combined with bodily gestures. Rather than dividing thoughts into separate nouns and verbs, these vocal calls delivered complete emotional messages designed to coordinate group hunting, calm aggression, and strengthen tribe unity. Their physical vocal anatomy was adapted for resonant group chanting across open landscapes.

Paragraph 4. The split between language and music occurred when early modern humans developed symbolic reasoning, breaking fluid calls into discrete referential words. While spoken language specialised in transmitting factual propositions and practical data, music retained its ancient power over human emotion and group solidarity. Mithen concludes that music was no evolutionary accident: it functioned as the essential social adhesive that allowed hominins to build large, cooperative communities and paved the path toward civilisation.
